questions.q: State the condition for a bipolar junction transistor to operate in the active region when used as a CE amplifier.
questions.a: The emitter-base junction must be forward-biased and the collector-base junction must be reverse-biased. A wrong answer (e.g., both junctions forward-biased) reveals the student confuses active region with saturation region, which would cause distortion and loss of amplification.

questions.q: Explain why the output voltage of a CE amplifier is 180° out of phase with the input voltage.
questions.a: When \(v_{in}\) increases, \(I_B\) increases → \(I_C = \beta I_B\) increases → voltage drop across \(R_L\) (\(I_C R_L\)) increases → \(V_{CE} = V_{CC} - I_C R_L\) decreases. Thus output voltage (\(V_{CE}\) or voltage across \(R_L\)) moves opposite to input. A wrong answer indicates the student memorizes "phase reversal" without understanding the voltage-divider action of \(R_L\) and the transistor.

questions.q: An npn transistor in CE configuration has \(\beta = 100\), input resistance \(r_i = 1.2\ \text{k}\Omega\), and load resistance \(R_L = 4.7\ \text{k}\Omega\). Calculate the voltage gain \(A_v\) and power gain \(A_p\).
questions.a: \(A_v = \beta \frac{R_L}{r_i} = 100 \times \frac{4700}{1200} = 391.7\) (dimensionless). \(A_p = \beta^2 \frac{R_L}{r_i} = 100^2 \times \frac{4700}{1200} = 3.92 \times 10^4\). A wrong answer (e.g., using \(R_L/r_i\) only) shows the student forgets the \(\beta\) factor in voltage gain or squares incorrectly for power gain.

questions.q: Given the output characteristics of an npn transistor in CE mode, a load line is drawn for \(V_{CC} = 12\ \text{V}\) and \(R_L = 2\ \text{k}\Omega\). The Q-point is chosen at \(I_C = 3\ \text{mA}, V_{CE} = 6\ \text{V}\). If the input signal causes \(I_B\) to vary by \(\pm 10\ \mu\text{A}\) and \(\beta = 100\), determine the peak-to-peak collector current swing and collector-emitter voltage swing.
questions.a: \(\Delta I_B = 20\ \mu\text{A}\) peak-to-peak → \(\Delta I_C = \beta \Delta I_B = 100 \times 20\ \mu\text{A} = 2\ \text{mA}\) peak-to-peak. \(\Delta V_{CE} = \Delta I_C \times R_L = 2\ \text{mA} \times 2\ \text{k}\Omega = 4\ \text{V}\) peak-to-peak. A wrong answer (e.g., using only peak values) reveals confusion between peak and peak-to-peak quantities in AC analysis.

questions.q: A student builds a CE amplifier with fixed bias (\(R_B\) only) and finds the Q-point shifts drastically when temperature rises. Evaluate why this happens and suggest a better biasing method.
questions.a: Fixed bias makes \(I_B\) (and thus \(I_C\)) highly temperature-dependent because \(V_{BE}\) decreases with temperature, increasing \(I_B = (V_{CC}-V_{BE})/R_B\). Voltage-divider bias (using \(R_1, R_2\) across \(V_{CC}\) with emitter resistor \(R_E\)) provides negative feedback that stabilizes the Q-point. A wrong evaluation shows the student does not understand thermal runaway and the role of \(R_E\) in stabilization.

questions.q: Design a simple experiment using a school laboratory CRO, function generator, and a BC547 transistor to demonstrate the phase reversal of a CE amplifier. Specify the key measurements and expected observations.
questions.a: Build voltage-divider bias CE amplifier with \(V_{CC}=9\ \text{V}\), \(R_L=2.2\ \text{k}\Omega\), \(R_1=47\ \text{k}\Omega\), \(R_2=10\ \text{k}\Omega\), \(R_E=1\ \text{k}\Omega\), coupling capacitors \(10\ \mu\text{F}\). Apply 1 kHz, 50 mVpp sine wave at input. Connect CRO CH1 to input (after \(C_{in}\)), CH2 to output (after \(C_{out}\)). Observe CH2 waveform inverted relative to CH1. Measure \(A_v = V_{out,pp}/V_{in,pp}\). A poor answer omits coupling capacitors, uses wrong bias, or expects no phase shift.
